custom: engravings of dogs and owls on people's houses
the streets are filled with skulls
consequence: the city's signature and its dread

custom: a traveller at the gate is given bread and water and a place by the hearth before any questions are asked; the host who shelters a guest gains standing before the city
consequence: turning a guest away hungry shames the house in the city's eyes and is told against it for years
source_ref: Mesopotamian hospitality custom (Sumerian and Akkadian wisdom literature: Instructions of Shuruppak; Counsels of Wisdom)

custom: the guest eats what is set before him; he does not open the host's storerooms; he keeps the house's peace and speaks no slander under its roof; news of the road is his thanks
consequence: a guest who violates the house that shelters him loses guest-right everywhere — no hearth will take him in
source_ref: Ancient Near Eastern guest-right custom (wisdom literature: Instructions of Shuruppak; the Mari letters on travellers and envoys)

custom: a gift received is a debt of honour: it is answered with a greater gift or a service; great houses count gifts owed and gifts given like debts
consequence: a gift left unanswered lowers the receiver below the giver; a gift given to bind a man puts a hook in him
source_ref: Near Eastern gift-exchange reciprocity (the Amarna letters' great-king gift exchange between brother-kings; the Mari letters' gift diplomacy)

custom: none enters the god's court unwashed: hands and feet washed; clean garments; contact with the dead abstained from for the set days; a zisurru flour circle bounds the pure ground
consequence: entering a temple impure draws reactions and refusal of entry (custom, city-life §4); rite-level gating awaits purity_required values (D-011)
source_ref: Mesopotamian cultic purity practice (ablutions and abstentions before temple entry; royal lustration — the 'house of washing'; zisurru flour circles — imported also by the notes)

custom: the first portion of every meal and the first pouring of every brew is set out for the god before any mouth eats or drinks; the temple's regular offering table is fed daily
consequence: food eaten without the god's portion is stolen from heaven; a house known to skip it loses the god's favour
source_ref: Mesopotamian temple offering practice (the ginu regular-offering corpus; offering tables and libations set before the deity)

custom: the dead are mourned aloud: lamentation priests and wailing mourners lead the grief; garments torn; dust on the head; the lament sung for the set days
consequence: a house that mourns quietly is judged to hold grudges against its own dead
source_ref: Mesopotamian mourning custom (the gala and kalu lamentation priests; the balag lament tradition)

custom: at the set time each month the dead are fed: a laid-out feast of food and drink for the ancestors; water poured for them; their names spoken so they do not fade
consequence: the neglected dead withdraw their blessing and walk restless; feeding them keeps peace between the living houses and the dead
source_ref: the kispum ancestral feast (Old Babylonian and later texts: regular offerings of food and water to the dead)

custom: the dead go provisioned: food and drink and vessels and ornaments laid in the grave for the road to the netherworld; the greater the dead the richer the outfitting
consequence: a robbed grave curses the robber and his house; provisioning the dead is a family duty and not a display
source_ref: the archaeological record (grave goods buried with the dead; the Royal Cemetery of Ur excavations)

custom: the oath is taken standing before witnesses: the swearer invokes heaven and earth and the great gods; oaths of state are sworn in the god's presence with hand on his emblem; before the throne one swears by the life of the king
consequence: perjury before the emblem is a sin against the god himself — the false swearer's name and house are cursed; unbroken oaths bind re-swearing (the one-oath rule)
source_ref: Mesopotamian oath and treaty practice (the 'by the life of the king' oath formula of the Old Babylonian letters; oaths sworn in the god's presence before his emblem)

custom: the legacy of kings is mummified and guarded here; the greatest kings are laid in massive underground catacombs to join the ancestors in the Kingdom of the Dead
consequence: the royal dead are the dynasty's proof and seat: to guard them is to hold the claim of kingship

custom: the biggest ancestor and underworld cult in the Empire; ritual scrolls for communicating with underworld spirits; the greatest temple built within the earth housing the great statue of the queen of the underworld
consequence: seekers of the underworld come here from all the lands; the dead are petitioned here as nowhere else in the Empire

custom: the barbarians keep the old shamanistic way of life that was part of Sumerian life before the urbanization; beside it their new customs of tribal warfare
consequence: they resist integration; where they rule the traces of city culture and economy rot and the farm animals run free
